title: Bethlehem Olivewood Crosses
subject: Evidence
stem:
Source row transformed: BARMATRIX Q#20313, Evidence, Attorney-client privilege, crime-fraud boundary.

Final Christian variation:

Lydia runs a small Bible-study gift cart at weekend retreats. Before selling a shipment of wooden crosses, she privately told her lawyer, Paul, “I am thinking about advertising these as carved from Bethlehem olivewood. Would that be legal? If that would be fraudulent, I will not use that description.” Paul researched the law and advised Lydia not to use the description.

Call: Are Lydia’s communications protected by attorney-client privilege?
call: Are Lydia’s communications protected by attorney-client privilege?

choices.A: Yes, but only if the customers later fail to prove substantial need for the communications.
choices.B: No, because any discussion of a potentially fraudulent advertisement triggers the crime-fraud exception.
choices.C: Yes, because she sought confidential legal advice to determine and avoid unlawful conduct, not to further a fraud.
choices.D: No, because Paul ultimately advised against the advertisement.

rightExplanation:
C is correct. Lydia was not asking Paul to help her carry out a fraud. She was asking whether the planned description would be lawful and stated that she would not use it if it was fraudulent. That makes the communication compliance-seeking legal advice.

Gold Key: Crime-fraud is purpose-based, not topic-based. A suspicious topic does not defeat privilege unless the client is using legal advice to commit, continue, or cover up a crime or fraud.

Silver Key: Do not stop at the word “fraud.” Name the axis: compliance advice versus abuse of legal advice. Lydia’s “if fraudulent, I will not do it” statement puts the communication on the compliance side.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: “Substantial need” is a real phrase, but it answers a different protection problem. This is wrong-frame / bait-doctrine.

c3.label: CLASH B vs C
c3.text: Axis = suspicious fraud topic versus purpose to seek compliance advice. The fact “If that would be fraudulent, I will not use that description” resolves the axis for C.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: D points the lawyer’s advice the wrong way. Advice against the act supports compliance, not loss of privilege.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Not needed after the Gold Key resolves the B/C clash.

studentScript: Call is privilege. Cut A because substantial need is the wrong protection. B and C fight on purpose: fraud-topic automatic exception versus compliance advice. The stem says she will not use the description if fraudulent. Keep C. Cut D because advice against the act points toward compliance.

A.signal: The answer imports substantial need, a neighboring discovery-protection idea, into an attorney-client privilege call.
A.lawyer: Substantial need is associated with work-product doctrine; it is not the override test for attorney-client communications.

B.signal: The word 'any' makes suspicious subject matter an automatic exception.
B.lawyer: Crime-fraud requires a communication made to further crime or fraud; asking how to avoid illegality is not enough.

C.signal: This choice answers the exact privilege call and tracks the compliance-advice fact.
C.lawyer: The communication is privileged because the client sought legal advice to determine legality and avoid fraud.

D.signal: The answer treats advice against the act as privilege-destroying, but that fact points toward compliance advice.
D.lawyer: A lawyer’s advice not to proceed does not defeat privilege; it supports the conclusion that the advice was not used to further fraud.

goldKeys.statement: Crime-fraud is purpose-based, not topic-based: privilege fails only when legal advice is sought to commit, continue, or cover up crime or fraud.
goldKeys.trigger: Client asks whether planned conduct would be fraudulent and says she will not do it if unlawful.
goldKeys.authority: FRE 501 common law; United States v. Zolin; Clark v. United States.

goldKeys.statement: Substantial need is a work-product concept; it is not the test for overriding attorney-client communications.
goldKeys.authority: Federal privilege and work-product doctrine distinction.

silverKeys.statement: When a privilege answer says 'fraud,' do not stop at the topic. Name the axis: compliance advice versus using the lawyer to further fraud.
silverKeys.trigger: Client says she will not proceed if the conduct is fraudulent.

remediation.title: Purpose beats suspicious topic
remediation.signal: Client asks whether a proposed act would be fraudulent.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the client is seeking compliance advice or help carrying out wrongdoing.
remediation.tinyRule: Crime-fraud needs furtherance; compliance advice remains privileged.
